# Data, Knowledge, and Representation {#sec-data-representations-world-models}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The limits of my language mean the limits of my world."
>
> — Ludwig Wittgenstein, *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus* [@Wittgenstein1922Tractatus, sec. 5.6]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *What does an AI-native design system need to know, where does that information come from, and how should it be represented?*

**Core thesis:** *Architecture data is expensive, heterogeneous, and sparse; representation choices dictate what design relationships remain visible and determine what automated methods can discover or miss.*
:::

A compiler schedule can reduce the number of instructions in a kernel and still slow the application because it increases memory traffic. A Verilog module can pass linting and still violate an interface contract or miss timing. To distinguish useful changes from plausible ones, an AI-native design system needs more than examples of code. It needs the architectural goals and specifications that define success, descriptions of the workloads that exercise the design, and observations that connect proposed changes to their consequences.

Some of this information already exists in specifications, block diagrams, design notes, source repositories, and prior experiments. Other information must be acquired through compilation, simulation, implementation tools, or measurement. The resulting collection reflects which designs and workloads the team could afford to examine, which tools it could access, and which failed runs it retained. More files do not necessarily cover more of the design problem.

The chapter first develops how to obtain and curate that information, then asks how to represent it for computational use. Raw observations, reusable explanations, and the state of the current design serve different purposes. Keeping them distinct lets an automated method use existing knowledge, request a missing observation, and retain what the result teaches without mistaking an old condition for a current one.

## Data Requirements for AI-Native Design

Consider a software-mapping question within Lighthouse: which compiler schedule should map a perception kernel onto a candidate neural processing unit (NPU)? A directory of schedules and a spreadsheet of cycle counts cannot answer it on their own. The workload description identifies the input shapes and required numerical behavior; the architecture specification and block diagram identify the available compute units, memories, and interfaces; and the design goals state which latency and resource constraints matter. These high-level sources determine what the team should measure before a simulator produces its first result.

The candidate schedule then connects that intent to executable work. A compiler intermediate representation (IR) exposes tile dimensions, dependencies, and data reuse. A simulator reports execution cycles, memory transfers, and stalls, while an input-output comparison checks whether the transformed kernel computes the required result. If the question also concerns the accelerator's implementation cost, synthesis and physical-design reports add area, timing, and power under their own library and operating assumptions. A design review may explain why an otherwise fast schedule was rejected because it complicates integration. No single source captures this whole argument, and collecting more examples of one source cannot replace a missing relationship to another.

What counts as one sample therefore depends on the question. A kernel-latency predictor needs an operator shape, schedule, and hardware target paired with an observed latency. A register-transfer level (RTL) generator instead needs a specification paired with an implementation and the checks performed on it. The sample's *context* records the conditions under which its contents apply; its *provenance* links those contents to their sources and to the transformations or tool runs that produced them. Joining records by candidate and workload identity lets transfer counts and stalls explain a timing result, while the recorded boundary keeps an isolated-kernel observation distinct from a complete extended-reality (XR) frame measurement.

A *representation* converts this engineering information into a form that computational methods can manipulate [@BengioEtAl2013RepresentationLearning]. It may make a prose requirement into a structured constraint linked to its specification, expose dependencies as a graph, or encode selected properties in a learned vector. Each choice preserves some relationships and omits others. The progression in @fig-architecture-data-progression connects collected sources to checked datasets, reusable knowledge, and the live state from which those task-specific views are built.

![**Architectural sources support different tasks through linked datasets, knowledge, and representations.** Checked datasets separate durable project knowledge from live candidate state before feeding native, structured, or learned views. Source identities, versions, and tool environments stay attached across every stage so that derived views never replace the native design files as the source of record. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-architecture-data-progression){#fig-architecture-data-progression width="100%" fig-alt="Flow diagram in which a left-to-right sequence begins with heterogeneous architecture sources, passes through a checked dataset, separates durable knowledge from current project state, and forms linked native, structured, and optional learned representations before method choice. A bar across the bottom states that source identity, versions, acquisition conditions, and links remain attached throughout. Native artifacts remain the source of record."}

The separate paths for knowledge and live state matter because a reusable design lesson can outlive the branch that produced it, while the current hardware, software, and constraints continue to change. Native sources remain available to resolve details that a derived view leaves out. For the mapping question, this organization starts with finding existing specifications, code, and observations, then identifying which missing measurements the team must acquire.

## Public Datasets and Their Limits {#sec-public-architecture-datasets}

Public repositories can reduce the cost of collecting data, but file count alone says little about fitness for a task. A large Verilog corpus may contain no timing reports or workload measurements. The first questions are what each sample observes, which design and workload populations it covers, and which properties were checked. The collections in @tbl-public-architecture-data illustrate different observation units and different effects of filtering, rather than interchangeable sources of architecture data.

| **Collection and observation unit** | **Supported task** | **Key missing context** | **Failed or rejected data status** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenRTLSet: an extracted Verilog module from public RTL or high-level synthesis (HLS) [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. | Module-level Verilog generation. | Project context, per-module functional checks, workload behavior, and physical measurements. | Failed conversions and their rejection reasons are not released. |
| RTL-Repo: a target-line completion with surrounding repository context [@AllamShalan2024RTLRepo]. | Multi-file Verilog completion. | Tool-checked behavior and physical results; reported split counts do not establish repository separation. | No design tool runs for the observation; filtered repositories are not retained. |
| CircuitNet: a back-end design run and retained layout [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet]. | Congestion, design rule violation, and IR-drop prediction. | Front-end software, workload behavior, and live project history. | 12,960 runs attempted; 10,242 layouts retained. Failure causes are not retained. |
| QuArch: an expert-validated architecture question-answer pair [@PrakashEtAl2025QuArch; @PrakashEtAl2025QuArchReasoning]. | Architecture knowledge and reasoning. | Executable design state and measured implementation behavior. | The first release excludes questions without definitive answers or with narrow scope. |
: **A dataset supports only the task and context carried by its observations.** Module code, repository context, executed layouts, and architecture questions serve distinct purposes and leave different parts of design decisions unobserved. {#tbl-public-architecture-data tbl-colwidths="[28,20,26,26]"}

CircuitNet's layouts can support a predictor of congestion or supply-grid IR drop,[^fn-ir-drop-c04] whereas QuArch's questions can probe architectural knowledge. Neither supplies the schedule-latency pairs needed for our mapping study. Their sizes must also be read in their own units: counting modules, layouts, or validated questions does not measure a common quantity of useful information. A narrow collection can be well suited to one component even when the team must obtain the rest of the study's information elsewhere.

[^fn-ir-drop-c04]: **IR drop**: The voltage decrease that occurs when current ($I$) flows through the resistance ($R$) of the power distribution network. Severe IR drop can cause transistors to switch too slowly, leading to timing violations or outright functional failures.

Collection filters help explain which designs survive into a public dataset. Public source code often needs several screening and compilation steps before it yields even a synthesizable hardware module.[^fn-hls-synthesizability-c04] The OpenRTLSet C/C++ collection path (@fig-public-code-to-rtl) traces how sharply an initially large repository pool narrows during that process.

[^fn-hls-synthesizability-c04]: **High-level synthesis (HLS) synthesizability**: High-level synthesis compiles algorithms expressed in high-level languages (such as C/C++) into RTL. Synthesizable code must stay within a restricted subset of the language. Dynamic memory allocation (for example, `malloc`), unbounded recursion, and operating system calls are generally unsupported, and pointer use is limited, because a circuit needs statically determinable memory sizes, register counts, and scheduling bounds.

```{python}
#| label: fig-public-code-to-rtl
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Building a Verilog corpus from public C/C++ code involves several filters.** The horizontal log-scale bar chart traces repository attrition in the OpenRTLSet C/C++ collection pipeline: approximately 103,000 permissively licensed repositories narrow to approximately 12,000 after synthesizability screening, and only approximately 1,000 successfully generate Verilog through Vitis HLS [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. The resulting 24,000 Verilog modules represent a distinct observation unit from the repositories shown. These counts reflect pipeline-specific tool filters rather than universal hardware synthesizability rates.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale horizontal bar chart showing three stages from the OpenRTLSet C and C++ collection pipeline. Approximately 103,000 permissively licensed repositories enter the pipeline, 12,000 remain after the authors' synthesizability screen, and 1,000 successfully generate Verilog through Vitis HLS."

# Source data: data/datasets/chapter4-openrtlset-funnel.csv
# (counts transcribed from OpenRTLSet, Section III-A, with per-row source columns)
import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(
    _root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter4-openrtlset-funnel.csv",
    encoding="utf-8",
) as fh:
    _funnel_rows = list(csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")))

# Only the repository-unit stages are plotted; the module count changes units.
_repo_rows = [row for row in _funnel_rows if row["unit"] == "repositories"]
assert len(_repo_rows) == 3
stages = [
    "Collected permissively\nlicensed C/C++ repositories",
    "After authors'\nsynthesizability screen",
    "Successful Vitis HLS\nto Verilog",
]
counts = [int(row["approximate_count"]) for row in _repo_rows]
display_counts = [f"≈{value:,}" for value in counts]
y = [2, 1, 0]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8, 2.0))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.38, right=0.92, top=0.9, bottom=0.2)

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(400, 300_000)

# Bars start at the axis floor and end exactly at each count.
bars = ax.barh(
    y,
    [value - 400 for value in counts],
    left=400,
    height=0.42,
    color=COLORS["workload"],
    edgecolor=COLORS["note_edge"],
    linewidth=0.8,
    zorder=2,
)

for x_value, y_value, label in zip(counts, y, display_counts):
    ax.text(
        x_value * 1.15,
        y_value,
        label,
        ha="left",
        va="center",
        fontsize=6.4,
        fontweight="bold",
        color=COLORS["workload_ink"],
    )

ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(stages, fontsize=6.2)
ax.set_xlabel("approximate repositories remaining (log scale)", fontsize=6.2)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.0, length=2.5, width=0.6)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0, pad=5)
ax.grid(axis="x", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6, zorder=1)

for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
```

The first large reduction occurs before Vitis HLS runs, when the authors screen for synthesizability; tool conversion narrows the pool further [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. General-purpose C/C++ can rely on dynamic memory, unbounded pointers, or system calls that high-level synthesis cannot map to a static circuit. The survivors therefore reflect both the source population and the tool's accepted language subset. They supply generated Verilog modules, not matching physical implementations or workload measurements. An abundant source pool can still leave expensive observations missing.

Because open repositories provide abundant source text but very few executed implementations, a foundation model pretrained on public corpora can learn syntax, circuit idioms, and documented design rules,[^fn-foundation-model-c04] yet still lack the evidence needed to apply those rules under project conditions. Assessing clock-domain crossings for metastability risk,[^fn-metastability-c04] managing power-grid voltage drops, and preventing combinational loops all require running verification and timing checks on the proposed design itself. That gap between syntax and verified implementation connects corpus quality directly to the evaluation bottleneck in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales, because generating a plausible artifact and qualifying it consume very different resources.

[^fn-metastability-c04]: **Metastability**: A transient state in which a storage element has not resolved to a valid logic level within the expected time. A setup or hold violation, including one caused by an asynchronous input, can produce it. Synchronizers reduce the probability that unresolved behavior reaches downstream logic; they do not eliminate the possibility of metastability.

[^fn-foundation-model-c04]: **Foundation model**: A model pretrained on broad data at scale and then adapted to many downstream tasks rather than trained for a single one [@BommasaniEtAl2021FoundationModels]. The term comes from machine learning, and this chapter treats such a model as one optional component inside a design system rather than as the design system itself.

Internal project archives can fill some of these gaps for in-house teams, subject to the access restrictions discussed in @sec-architecture-data-access. ChipNeMo, for example, adapts a language model using proprietary chip-design material for engineering assistance, electronic design automation (EDA) script generation, and bug summarization [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]. Using internal material improves domain performance without making that material publicly reproducible, so an evaluation still has to state which evidence an independent reviewer can inspect.

For the mapping study, compatible prior runs would save work only if their kernels, schedules, hardware targets, and checks match the intended use. Remaining gaps require new observations, and the tools that produce them determine both their cost and the conditions they can cover.

## Collecting Architectural Data

Launching a data-collection sweep without an explicit plan can burn weeks of cluster compute and tool licenses while leaving the study's central question unanswered. A team can run thousands of cycle simulations on a single convenient input shape, or synthesize netlists at one nominal corner, only to discover that the decisive memory-traffic or timing bottleneck was never exercised. Even in a software-focused experiment like the Lighthouse mapping study, testing a schedule change requires new compilation, numerical verification, and simulator execution. Planning that collection therefore requires balancing three coupled choices: the tool path used to evaluate a candidate, the compute and engineering resources required per sample, and the workloads or operating conditions covered.

### Choosing Tools That Can See the Bottleneck

A fast evaluation tool can miss the effect that reverses a design comparison. A trace replay may omit timing feedback that changes bus contention, while a pre-layout timing estimate omits routed interconnect delays. In the Lighthouse mapping study, comparing schedules requires observations of computation and data movement; estimating the accelerator's physical cost requires a different tool path. The source categories in @tbl-observation-source-limits make that choice explicit by pairing what a source observes with what it leaves unresolved.

| **Source** | **Useful for** | **Important limit to represent** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical model | Fast sensitivity studies and early bounds. | Simplifying equations, calibration range, and omitted interactions. |
| Trace-driven or cycle-level simulator | Memory traffic, execution cycles, stalls, and contention within the model. | Trace capture and feedback limits, unsupported states, calibration, and runtime. |
| RTL or gate-level simulation | Logic and interface behavior under the exercised testbench; modeled cell delays where included. | Stimulus coverage and physical effects absent from the simulation model. |
| Formal analysis | Proof, counterexample, bounded result, or inconclusive status for a property. | Assumptions, abstraction, proof bounds, and whether the property can pass without exercising the intended behavior. |
| Synthesis, timing, and power analysis | Technology-mapped area, static timing analysis (STA), and power estimates. | Libraries, operating corners, constraints, activity assumptions, and physical approximations. |
| Place-and-route and physical verification | Routed geometry, extracted delays, congestion, and implementation checks. | Floorplan state, operating modes, manufacturing models, and waived checks. |
| Field-programmable gate array (FPGA), emulation, or fabricated silicon | Execution on a mapped or physical implementation. | Mapping and test conditions, limited observability, and which results transfer to the target implementation. |
: **Every observation source has a useful scope and a blind spot.** Recording both ensures appropriate tool selection and qualification in downstream chapters. {#tbl-observation-source-limits tbl-colwidths="[22,36,42]"}

A clean result from one tool therefore never substitutes for an unmodeled check in another. A timing-closure report on a gate-level netlist says nothing about routed power-grid droop, and a transaction-level throughput estimate does not bound cycle-accurate tail latency when flits contend for the same link. Attaching these modeling limits to each observation lets a downstream method distinguish a fast early proxy from a measurement of the target property.

Even within a single tool, hardware measurements depend on the operating conditions under which they were obtained. In an illustrative multiplier example, suppose static timing analysis reports a 1.1\ ns cycle time at an assumed typical corner (0.85\ V, $25^\circ\text{C}$), while evaluating that same design at a second assumed corner (0.72\ V, $125^\circ\text{C}$) or under a different clock-tree skew target changes whether the implementation closes timing.[^fn-timing-closure-c04] Although these hypothetical values neither measure a particular multiplier or foundry process nor fix the size of a timing violation, they show why a timing or power label is incomplete without the implementation and analysis conditions that produced it.

[^fn-timing-closure-c04]: **Timing closure and operating corners**: Timing closure establishes that the analyzed paths meet their specified timing requirements, including setup and hold, under the selected models and constraints. Process, voltage, and temperature affect delays; the limiting corner can differ by path and check. Passing the required corners supports those timing claims, not a guarantee against every silicon failure.

The source and its operating conditions thus determine which observation a run can supply. They also determine its acquisition cost: another timing corner, workload, or implementation can require another tool run rather than another column extracted from an existing log.

### The Compute and License Cost of Collecting Samples

In the Lighthouse mapping study, sample acquisition begins well before timed execution, because each candidate schedule must compile for the target, pass output correctness checks, and load into the evaluation environment before a simulator or hardware run can return latency and diagnostic counters. While preparing the compiler backend or calibrating the accelerator model is a shared upfront investment, compilation, testing, execution, and diagnosis accumulate per candidate and multiply across repeated runs and workload shapes, so a dataset budget that counts only the final timing call misses much of the work required to produce a usable label.

Once a candidate clears compilation and correctness checks, timed simulation often dominates the per-sample cost. We can quantify the effect of execution coverage independently of a particular Lighthouse candidate by considering an illustrative 1\ GHz target, a 1\ s measured interval, 0.2\ s of warmup, a simulator rate of 100,000 target cycles per wall-clock second, three repetitions, and four workloads.

```{python}
#| echo: false

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

# Source data: data/datasets/chapter4-simulation-time-explosion.csv

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(
    _root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter4-simulation-time-explosion.csv",
    encoding="utf-8",
) as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    _simulation_cost_rows = list(csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")))

_one_second_row = next(
    row
    for row in _simulation_cost_rows
    if row["target_workload_duration"] == "1 s"
)
measurement_cycles = int(_one_second_row["target_cycles_at_1ghz"])
warmup_cycles = measurement_cycles // 5
simulator_rate = 100_000
repetitions = 3
workloads = 4
single_measurement_hours = measurement_cycles / simulator_rate / 3_600
total_target_cycles = (
    (warmup_cycles + measurement_cycles) * repetitions * workloads
)
total_serial_hours = total_target_cycles / simulator_rate / 3_600
assert _one_second_row["wall_time_at_100kcycle_s"] == "2.8 h"
assert round(total_target_cycles / 1e9, 1) == 14.4
assert round(total_serial_hours) == 40
```

During a single measured interval of 1\ s, a 1\ GHz target executes one billion cycles ($10^9$). At an assumed simulator rate of 100,000 target cycles per wall-clock second, simulating that single second takes roughly 2.8\ hours. Serial execution cost $T_{\text{serial}}$ combines target warmup cycles $C_{\text{warmup}}$, target measurement cycles $C_{\text{measure}}$, repetition count $R$, workload count $W$, and simulator throughput $v_{\text{sim}}$:

$$
T_{\text{serial}} =
\frac{(C_{\text{warmup}} + C_{\text{measure}}) \times R \times W}
{v_{\text{sim}}}.
$${#eq-serial-execution-cost}

If we evaluate four workloads across three repetitions under the assumptions in @eq-serial-execution-cost, the study executes 14.4 billion target cycles and consumes forty serial simulator hours.[^fn-simulation-warmup-c04]

[^fn-simulation-warmup-c04]: **Simulation warmup**: Architectural simulators begin execution with uninitialized (cold) state in caches, branch target buffers, translation lookaside buffers (TLBs), and prefetchers. Simulating an initial interval ($C_{\text{warmup}}$) without gathering statistics warms up internal microarchitectural structures to realistic steady-state hit rates before the actual measurement window begins.

Those forty hours represent accumulated simulator runtime for one candidate configuration. Running jobs in parallel across a cluster can shorten wall-clock collection time when compute nodes and licenses permit, but it does not reduce total machine time, and shared setup, compilation, correctness checks, queueing, and failure diagnosis add further cost beyond the execution estimate.

Replacing direct simulation with a fast surrogate does not eliminate that upfront acquisition budget either. Even if a surrogate evaluates a candidate in an illustrative two milliseconds, it still requires reference tool runs for training and calibration, whose collection can consume days or weeks of cluster compute. In BOOM-Explorer, for example, the authors built an offline dataset of 994 sampled microarchitectural configurations, and running the very-large-scale integration flow for each design took from about six to more than fourteen hours [@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer]. At those per-sample costs, sweeping millions of variations requires a staged acquisition strategy rather than exhaustive evaluation.

Because every observation carries a real compute and engineering price, recording resource consumption alongside the measurements helps the team budget further collection. Execution time, memory footprint, license demand, and human debugging effort determine which evaluation paths remain practical at different scales, while the run's operating conditions and check status establish what that expenditure actually proved. Together, these details let a later user judge both whether an observation is trustworthy and what obtaining comparable samples would cost (@tbl-architecture-observations-not-labels).

| **Dataset simplification** | **Architecture sample** | **Consequence for later use** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cheap acquisition** | Results require scarce licenses, long tool runs, fabrication, setup, diagnosis, and expert review. | Records must capture resources and human work required to obtain the result. |
| **Fixed ground-truth label** | Tools return results for named properties at stated fidelities under recorded conditions. | Properties, checks, fidelities, and conditions must be preserved for interpretation. |
| **Independent, interchangeable rows** | Results frequently share ancestors, generated artifacts, traces, images, seeds, or earlier decisions. | Lineage must be preserved to avoid counting dependent results as independent support. |
| **Missing data without structure** | Failed, timed-out, and rejected runs are selectively lost; some violations reveal only threshold crossings. | Run status, failure reasons, and censored bounds must be retained rather than learning only from survivors. |
| **Matching attributes imply comparability** | Two rows support comparison only when candidate identities, permitted differences, workloads, and tool paths match. | Results with uncontrolled differences must be treated as advisory context rather than matched comparisons. |
: **Architecture samples are costly, conditioned results.** Their meaning and comparability depend on lineage, property checks, acquisition status, and matched study conditions. {#tbl-architecture-observations-not-labels tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

The distinction between independent rows and shared lineage is especially important for budgeting. Repeating a run can characterize its variability without adding a new workload or design. The team must decide which of those uncertainties its next observation needs to resolve.

### Workload Coverage and Representative Sampling

Once the price of a single evaluation is clear, the next question is which workload executions deserve that budget. Static hardware descriptions show what a system can execute, but running workloads determine which datapaths become active, which queues saturate, and which memory banks stall. Because full applications run for billions of cycles, a short trace slice is useful only if it captures the runtime behavior that governs the architectural decision.

In our Lighthouse XR workload, what a sample must include depends on the system boundary under test. An isolated kernel measurement needs its input tensor shape, data type, and schedule, whereas a full-frame measurement also needs the surrounding pipeline stages and their execution overlap. Because the subsystem's 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) envelope applies to all work inside that boundary, an isolated kernel that runs fast on its own may still wait for upstream inputs or contend with rendering when integrated. The dataset must therefore distinguish isolated-kernel observations from frame-level observations instead of treating both as interchangeable labels for the same target.

Even at the right boundary, workload coverage has to match the metric being evaluated. A trace collection chosen to estimate average throughput can miss brief memory-bus stalls that decide whether a perception frame meets its real-time deadline. Before selecting representative intervals, an evaluation plan has to identify which workload behaviors could flip the architectural conclusion.

System performance, power dissipation, and thermal behavior are joint outcomes $y = f(x, w)$ of the hardware configuration $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and the dynamic workload feature vector $w \in \mathcal{W}$. Changing the application software or moving to a different execution phase can shift a hardware candidate from compute-bound to memory-bound. To capture these runtime shifts without paying for full-trace simulation, architects compress execution traces into compact feature representations.

SimPoint, for example, builds basic block vectors ($w_{\text{BBV}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$) by counting how often each static basic block executes during fixed instruction intervals (such as $10^7$ or $10^8$ instructions), weighting those counts by static block length, and normalizing across the interval [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint].[^fn-simpoint-c04] Projecting those interval vectors into a lower-dimensional space (for example, via random projection) and clustering them with $k$-means identifies recurring program phases, allowing a small set of weighted simulation intervals (SimPoints) to estimate full-trace behavior.

[^fn-simpoint-c04]: **SimPoint**: A methodology that clusters program-execution intervals and selects representatives for weighted simulation estimates. It can reduce simulation cost; accuracy depends on the selected intervals, target metrics, and evaluation conditions.

Clustering program phases reduces simulation cost, but it does not automatically supply an error bound for a new design; the architect still has to verify how accurately the selected intervals estimate the target metrics. When a study requires explicit statistical confidence intervals over sampled execution slices, systematic sampling methods such as SMARTS compute those bounds directly under their sampling assumptions [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS].

For modern accelerator and transformer workloads, compact workload descriptors extend beyond basic block counts to capture key-value cache footprints and decoding burst lengths. Together with basic block vectors and memory-stride histograms, these features can condition a learned performance predictor on runtime workload behavior and represent the workload portion of a design loop's state (@sec-hardware-representation-formats).

Whether a team can reuse captured traces or phase descriptors across candidates depends on whether the compiler output changes. In the Lighthouse mapping study, a new loop tiling or scheduling choice alters the memory-access stream itself, so replaying an old schedule's trace would not evaluate the new schedule; the workload inputs and comparison window stay matched, but each candidate must generate its own trace. Basic block vectors likewise stay bound to the compiled binary, collection policy, frame identifiers, and execution parameters that produced them. That dependency separates a software-changing mapping study from a hardware cache study that holds the compiled software image fixed across candidates.

These dependencies also constrain collection over time. If a compiler release or simulator flag changes between baseline and candidate runs, the difference may reflect the collection environment rather than the intended design change. The collection plan must preserve matched conditions or explicitly separate the affected runs. The next task is assembling those observations into a dataset whose coverage and grouping match the comparison.

## Constructing Architecture Datasets

Provenance records keep a single observation intact, but building an architectural dataset requires deciding which observations belong together and which parts of the design space they should cover. Because the acquisition costs derived earlier limit how many runs a team can afford, simply collecting convenient simulation logs and Verilog files often leaves the cases that distinguish competing designs untested.

The target population and the collected sample can differ substantially. A deployment workload may encounter shapes and execution phases in proportions unlike those in a convenient trace archive. A hardware sweep may concentrate on designs that compile quickly or fit an available library. These choices shape the data distribution, meaning which combinations of designs, workloads, and conditions appear and how frequently. The collection plan must expose that selection so the team can distinguish repeated observations of familiar cases from coverage of the cases its decision concerns.

In our Lighthouse mapping study, for example, the collection plan must cover the operator shapes and schedules that could flip which candidate wins. If a team evaluates dozens of tile sizes on a single convenient matrix shape, the rest of the perception workload remains unrepresented. A useful initial dataset instead spans distinct reuse patterns and working-set sizes, including shapes that push against the target's local memory limits, while reserving evaluation budget to check whether an apparent kernel speedup survives integration into the full frame workload.

Whether a dataset is adequate therefore depends on the specific comparison it has to resolve. More repetitions characterize run-to-run variation, new input shapes close a workload coverage gap, and another hardware target tests cross-platform transfer; all three compete for the same acquisition budget and cannot substitute for one another. In the smaller cache study, the observations must resolve whether a candidate improves on the baseline while respecting static random-access memory (SRAM) area and power limits. Whenever the available observations leave a comparison undecided, the next sample should target the specific uncertainty blocking that decision.

When the dataset supports a learned predictor, its examples serve different roles. Training examples fit the predictor's relationship between inputs and observed outputs; held-out evaluation examples assess its predictions on the kinds of unseen cases the study intends to handle. Those evaluation results must not steer fitting or the choice of additional training samples, because they would then help shape the predictor they are meant to assess.

### Multi-Fidelity Sampling

Because cycle-accurate simulation and physical layout are too slow to run on every candidate while analytical formulas are too coarse to certify a winner, teams often combine cheap and expensive evaluations in the same dataset. Done carelessly, pooling rough roofline bounds and cycle-accurate measurements into a single unlabeled latency column teaches a predictor to treat approximation error as hardware behavior. *Multi-fidelity sampling* stretches a fixed acquisition budget safely by pairing inexpensive estimates with costly simulations or implementation runs, provided the sources estimate the same output or have an explicit relationship between their outputs [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity] and each row records which tool produced it. Within that budget, active learning can allocate further observations by selecting examples expected to improve a model or reduce uncertainty [@Settles2009ActiveLearning], although its usefulness depends on whether those selections repay their acquisition cost.

In the mapping study, inexpensive analytical estimates can screen many candidate schedules while cycle-level evaluations examine selected candidates near constraint boundaries or decision crossovers, leaving unvisited regions unsupported. When an adaptive selection policy picks those follow-up samples from earlier results, the dataset must also record its selection rules, candidate pools, and available observations; otherwise, a later evaluation cannot tell whether its test cases already steered the sampling loop [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout].

### Cleaning Logs and Preventing Train-Test Leakage

Even carefully collected tool runs can be ruined during dataset assembly if a regular-expression log parser silently turns a negative timing slack or missing report into `0.0`, or if a split intended to test new design families scatters variants from the same Chisel or SystemVerilog generator template across training and evaluation partitions. Curation is what prevents those pipeline bugs from masquerading as clean training data. In the mapping dataset, each row identifies a kernel, input shape, schedule, and hardware target, and links to its compiled artifact, correctness result, repeated timings, and diagnostic counters, with consistent units, grouped repetitions, and missing results kept distinct from measured zeros. The source kernel and transformation history also supply the grouping keys needed for evaluation splits, because holding out new schedules for a familiar kernel tests a different capability from holding out an operator family that never appeared in training.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import json as _json4et
from pathlib import Path as _Path4et
import _python.plots as _ap4et

_et15 = _json4et.loads(
    (_Path4et(_ap4et.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
     / "data" / "studies" / "15-errata-title-reuse" / "summary.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
et15_entries = f"{_et15['entries']:,}"
et15_families = _et15["families"]
et15_shared = f"{_et15['entries_with_title_shared_across_families']:,}"
et15_shared_pct = f"{100 * _et15['shared_entry_fraction']:.1f}"
et15_groups = _et15["groups_appearing_in_multiple_families"]
```

Those grouping keys matter because training examples in a hardware table are rarely independent and identically distributed. Multiple rows often share a design ancestor, generated artifact, workload trace, or software image, and repeated evaluations of a single schedule measure run-to-run variation rather than independent programs. Published processor errata show the same lineage overlap between product lines: of the `{python} et15_entries` erratum entries documented for `{python} et15_families` Intel and AMD CPU families in @sec-what-architect-owns, `{python} et15_shared` entries (`{python} et15_shared_pct`%) share a case-and-whitespace-normalized title with at least one other family across `{python} et15_groups` multi-family title groups [@Intel2020XeonScalableSpecUpdate; @AMD2023Family17h00hRevisionGuide]. When the dataset records those lineage links explicitly, an evaluation split can test the intended form of transfer and prevent a high row count from disguising a narrow set of underlying designs.

Protected evaluation splits must therefore match the intended unseen cases, whether new configurations within a known family, new design families, workloads, software revisions, or time periods [@KapoorNarayanan2023Leakage]. Configurations from a parameterized hardware description language (HDL) generator often share circuit structure. Holding out configurations from that generator can legitimately test prediction within its design family, but does not establish transfer to a new family. A claim about new families requires separating the generating templates as well as the table rows.

Pipeline construction must also guard against *data contamination*, because exposure to public hardware benchmarks during training can inflate evaluation scores through memorization rather than genuine generalization to new designs [@WangEtAl2025VeriContaminated; @Balloccu2024Leakage]. Because private testbenches, repository-disjoint splits, and behavior-preserving transformations of test artifacts address different exposure risks, no single measure is mandatory or sufficient for every study; instead, a dataset record should state which exposure paths were examined, what each measure protects, and whether any transformed tasks still test the claimed capability.

Synthetic training examples require similar qualification matched to their intended use, since treating unverified generator outputs as measured observations can mislead downstream learning [@VanBreugelEtAl2023SyntheticData]. Methods such as CraftRTL use synthetic Verilog examples to repair model errors [@LiuEtAl2024CraftRTL], yet passing syntax checks does not establish functional behavior, and passing functional tests says nothing about timing or power. A dataset can retain examples at any of these stages if it records the generator identity, intended task, and completed checks, while reserving physical evaluation for labels that make a physical claim.

Finally, the extraction scripts that assemble tool outputs into table columns require the same scrutiny as the splits, because upstream parsing bugs can trigger *data cascades* that surface only as delayed errors in downstream work [@SambasivanEtAl2021DataCascades]. In architecture studies, a parser that drops a minus sign on timing slack or classifies license exhaustion as a design failure turns raw tool returns into mislabeled training examples, introducing label noise that must be caught and corrected before it distorts what a model learns [@NorthcuttJiangChuang2021ConfidentLearning]. An unrecorded compiler flag or source transformation can similarly alter a comparison's meaning without leaving a trace in the feature columns. When the pipeline links every computed attribute back to its raw tool returns and extraction scripts, a reviewer can detect such bugs and determine which conclusions they affect.

### Preserving Failed and Censored Execution Runs

Discarding failed tool runs or collapsing every non-passing return into a single `fail` bit corrupts a dataset in two ways: dropping unroutable or timing-violating layouts blinds a surrogate predictor to the physical feasibility boundary, while logging a dropped FlexLM license connection as a design failure teaches an optimizer to avoid a valid region of the search space. To keep those cases distinct, a dataset pipeline must record what an evaluation attempt actually established across five outcome classes:

- *Infrastructure faults* (such as floating-license exhaustion or network interruption) identify problems with the execution environment rather than an infeasible design, although a simulator crash still requires diagnosis before a team assigns it to this category and chooses a repair or retry policy.
- *Syntax and typing defects* (such as undeclared wires or bitwidth mismatches) identify errors in a proposed artifact, where repair may require changing the artifact, its generator, or the transformation that produced it.
- *Constraint violations* (such as negative setup slack, unroutability, or exceeded power-delivery-network IR-drop limits) identify a failed requirement under the recorded implementation and tool conditions. They constrain reuse under those conditions without proving that every implementation of the architecture must fail.
- *Formal verification results* distinguish proofs, counterexamples, bounded results, and inconclusive returns, where each retains its property, assumptions, and proof scope because a bounded check cannot establish behavior beyond its horizon.
- *Resource-limit stops* retain the elapsed budget, partial results, and unresolved property when a timeout could reflect candidate complexity, tool behavior, or infrastructure rather than identifying a single cause on its own.

In a compiler-schedule search, a fast schedule that computes the wrong answer is not a valid speedup, whereas an unexplained compiler crash does not prove that the schedule is infeasible on the target hardware. Retaining the inputs, raw tool returns, and failure classification together lets diagnostic scripts and training pipelines separate environment faults from broken candidates.

For physical design runs, training a surrogate exclusively on clean signoff runs omits measured timing and routing violations at the feasibility boundary. Because those omitted outcomes depend directly on the quantities being predicted, this selection introduces survivorship bias [@Rubin1976InferenceMissingData].

A censored observation establishes a bound on a named quantity rather than its exact value.[^fn-censored-c04] A timed-out simulation might establish $y \ge y_{\text{limit}}$ for dynamic execution latency, for example, whereas an EDA tool timeout supplies no such bound on circuit path delay because an incomplete place-and-route run lacks extracted layout parasitics. Leaving those physical interconnect delays unbounded requires downstream predictive and search methods to distinguish bounded simulation timeouts from unresolved physical runs (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).

[^fn-censored-c04]: **Censored observation**: The result establishes only that a value lies above or below a threshold rather than reporting the value itself [@KleinMoeschberger2003Survival]. A failed target-frequency test is left-censored because it establishes that maximum sustainable frequency lies below the target.

A versioned execution history separates attempt status, candidate outcome, and project updates so that data-cleaning routines do not conflate tool failures with design evidence (@fig-execution-history). With all three recorded separately, a later reader or search method can distinguish a completed check that rejected a candidate from an aborted attempt that left it unresolved.

![**Execution history tracking preserves status, outcome, and cost attributes.** Separating tool execution status from candidate qualification and project commits keeps automated workflows from discarding useful negative evidence. Recorded attempt attributes and failure reasons let later methods tell whether an earlier failure reflects a physical design limit or an obsolete tool setup. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-execution-history){#fig-execution-history width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram of a versioned execution history with separate attempt status, candidate outcome, and project update attributes. One completed attempt advances a candidate and creates a new project version. A second completed attempt leaves the candidate rejected or unresolved and makes no project update. A third attempt completes on stale inputs, which yields no usable candidate outcome for the current comparison and leaves project state unchanged."}

A single pass/fail bit cannot represent the stale-input path, in which the tool exits cleanly and the run looks successful even though its inputs no longer match the active baseline, yielding no usable outcome for the current comparison. That separation between attempt status and candidate outcome stops an automated search from treating a stale success as a valid baseline or mistaking a timeout for an architectural refutation. In our mapping study, for instance, an old schedule's timing result can remain useful training material for a broad cost model even after a new compiler release disqualifies it as a matched baseline comparison; because its value depends on how later work intends to use it and which conditions changed, an explicit execution history preserves the run for training without presenting it as a current measurement.

Pairing failure labels with root-cause diagnostics lets later work distinguish environment faults from design violations under the tested conditions (@tbl-negative-traces), without treating an earlier boundary as permanent after the design or operating conditions change.

| **Failed run or rejected alternative** | **Preserved information** | **How later work should use it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Synthesis or timing violation** | Candidate, constraints, process assumptions, and failing paths. | Reconsider the candidate only after checking whether relevant conditions still apply. |
| **Unroutable or power failure** | Netlist, placement conditions, density, congestion, or IR-drop result. | Identify the affected region without treating the failure as characteristic of all similar designs. |
| **Proxy improvement overturned** | Cheap estimate, later observation, and precise divergence conditions. | Reassess the proxy's useful scope before attempting reuse. |
| **Tool failure or crash** | Command, inputs, environment identity, logs, and failure classification. | Diagnose the cause; repair infrastructure when established as the cause. Otherwise retain unresolved status until evidence supports classification. |
| **Coverage gap** | Missing workload, input, scenario, or architecture class. | Mark the strict boundary of the result rather than filling it with assumptions. |
| **Reviewer rejection** | Candidate, stated reason, risk, schedule, integration concern, and owner. | Preserve rationale and revisit only when relevant conditions fundamentally change. |
| **Waiver or exception** | Violated rule, justification, scope, owner, and expiration condition. | Prevent repeated work while keeping the granted exception visible. |
: **Rejected work remains useful when conditions are systematically recorded.** Explicit failure conditions allow subsequent architects to determine whether historical boundaries still apply. {#tbl-negative-traces tbl-colwidths="[26,34,40]"}

These diagnostic records also point to what the next experiment should test. In the mapping study, a schedule whose buffers exceed local-memory capacity directly motivates trying a smaller tile or a different staging pattern; the diagnosed failure gives the next run a clear hypothesis while leaving open which revision will succeed.

## Turning Data into Reusable Design Knowledge

While curated observations establish what happened under particular test conditions, turning those records into durable architectural knowledge requires explaining why the result occurred well enough to guide another decision. Suppose, as an illustrative interpretation rather than a reported Lighthouse result, that evaluations in our mapping study found one schedule reduced both off-chip transfers and execution time on matched inputs, suggesting that its tiling kept intermediate data in local memory for reuse. Because the timing result alone does not establish that mechanism, an architect needs the transfer counts, stall behavior, and generated schedule to test that explanation against alternatives such as a change in parallelism or instruction overhead.

Once checked, the reusable lesson states when that schedule helps, showing that it accelerates shapes whose working sets fit in the available local memory whereas larger shapes require additional off-chip transfers and lose the benefit. Contrasting those passing and spilling cases turns an isolated ranking into a conditional explanation, provided the supporting runs, counterexamples, and remaining uncertainty stay linked to it. Without those links, a later method may reuse the winning tile size after the workload or memory organization has changed, even though the physical reason it worked no longer applies.

That boundary separates three kinds of project records: *raw data* captures source observations, *durable knowledge* encompasses reusable design principles, checked specifications, and architectural explanations, and *live project state* identifies the hardware, software, workload, and constraints governing current work. An explanation can remain useful long after the specific candidate that produced it has changed, but applying it to new work requires checking whether current conditions still match. A learned model may suggest a familiar scheduling pattern from its training corpus, while the active compiler artifacts and workload description establish whether that pattern actually applies to the candidate under test. The information sources in @tbl-knowledge-objects contribute distinct parts of this judgment.

| **Information source** | **What it contributes** | **What to check before reuse** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Trained-model weights** | Learned statistical regularities and general concepts. | Use as prior knowledge; consult project sources for the current design and constraints. |
| **Retrieved material** | Manuals, papers, examples, and project documents. | Check the underlying source and whether its version applies to the intended use. |
| **In-context working set** | Instructions, selected sources, current state, and operational examples. | Check which sources were supplied. Text in a model's context does not itself update the design. |
| **Defined comparison** | Question, comparator, scope, permitted changes, constraints, budget, and stop rules. | Confirm that the comparison still uses the intended baseline and permits the proposed change. |
| **Design and software artifacts** | Configuration, generated hardware, software images, manifests, and constraints. | Identify the hardware and software versions being evaluated, and distinguish checks already completed from those still required. |
| **Workload data** | Traces, profiles, observed population, phase definitions, and sampling policy. | Check whether the captured inputs and phases cover the behavior relevant to the new question. |
| **Project history** | Prior candidates, tool runs, failures, decisions, and rationale linked to conditions. | Check whether the conditions supporting an earlier conclusion still apply. |
: **Reusing knowledge requires checking the information that makes it applicable.** Models, documents, artifacts, and observations contribute different parts of that judgment; none substitutes for all the others. {#tbl-knowledge-objects tbl-colwidths="[20,34,46]"}

These sources age at different rates and become outdated for different reasons. A general scheduling principle may remain valid while the interface specification needed to apply it has changed, and allowing an obsolete constraint into an active evaluation loop can split a proposal from the checks meant to verify it.[^fn-split-brain-c04] When a generator pulls a bus width or clock frequency from outdated documentation while targeting the current implementation, its proposal can be syntactically clean and internally consistent while violating the parameters governing the rest of the system (@fig-split-brain-causality).

[^fn-split-brain-c04]: **Stale constraint optimization**: A proposal is generated or evaluated against an outdated requirement. It may pass checks using that same stale requirement while violating the current design's interface, timing, or functional obligations.

![**Outdated specifications can produce internally consistent designs that conflict with the current system.** When a generator or retriever reads frozen reference files after the active project has updated its interfaces, the resulting proposal can satisfy local syntax while violating current system constraints. Freshness and version checks catch that divergence before tool dispatch. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-split-brain-causality){#fig-split-brain-causality width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram in which a stale reference state and a current project state lead to an incompatible proposal. Version and freshness checks expose the mismatch before the proposal reaches a costly tool flow."}

A stale interface assumption easily survives syntax parsing and isolated module synthesis because neither check inspects the system-level boundary, so the mismatch usually surfaces during integration or later, when repair is most expensive. Checking input identities and version hashes before launching simulator or synthesis runs catches that drift early, although confirming full interface compatibility still requires functional checks against the active design.

Updates to live project state carry their own compute, storage, license, and review costs. Whenever a compiler release, a new workload capture, or a revised bus specification makes part of the recorded knowledge inapplicable, the team needs a way to detect what went stale and decide which records to refresh. A smaller set of verified, up-to-date sources is therefore more useful to an active design loop than a broad archive whose applicability is unclear, and the next step is encoding those verified sources into computational forms that predictors, generators, and optimizers can consume.

## Machine-Usable Design Representations {#sec-hardware-representation-formats}

A design specification may state a latency goal, a block diagram may show which units share a memory, and a review note may explain why an interface must remain fixed. A method needs access to those relationships before it proposes a change. A structured constraint can pair the latency target with its workload boundary and source passage; a graph can expose the shared memory and its connected units; a linked decision record can explain the frozen interface. These views make high-level information usable without pretending that extracting a requirement proves it is satisfied. The original specification and rationale remain available when a compact encoding leaves an ambiguity unresolved.

Availability matters as much as structure. Feeding every column of a curated dataset into a model can leak post-execution measurements into a pre-execution predictor. A latency surrogate trained with simulator stall cycles among its inputs may look accurate on held-out rows yet be unusable before the simulator has run. For the mapping study, a pre-execution representation can expose operator shape, data type, loop organization, tile sizes, and target-memory parameters, while measured latency supplies the training target. Dynamic transfers and stalls belong to post-run diagnosis unless an upstream model estimates them first. AutoTVM illustrates this distinction by feeding its cost models features extracted from low-level loop programs or learned representations of their syntax trees [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM].

A generator, by contrast, needs a representation it can legally modify. A vector of tile sizes describes alternatives within a fixed schedule template, but proposing a different ordering or fusion of operations requires access to data dependencies and supported transformations so that the resulting schedule maps cleanly to compiler inputs and preserves numerical behavior. In our Lighthouse study, the same data-design question asks what representations a prospective accelerator target requires, without assuming that a trained cost model or compiler backend is already in place.

### Structure Beyond Token Sequences

Hardware description languages illustrate the consequences of this representation choice for circuits. SystemVerilog and VHSIC Hardware Description Language (VHDL) encode concurrent hardware in linear text, yet token order does not directly expose circuit connectivity or timing relationships because two signals that sit far apart in a source file may share the same critical path. A model consuming RTL as a flat token sequence must reconstruct those relationships from identifiers, whereas a circuit graph exposes connectivity directly and links to cell libraries and constraint files for the electrical context absent from the RTL. Even so, neither representation alone establishes capacitive fanout loading, clock-domain crossing safety, or setup and hold timing across physical operating corners.[^fn-setup-hold-c04]

[^fn-setup-hold-c04]: **Setup and hold times**: Timing requirements for a register's data input around the sampling clock edge. Setup time specifies how long the data must be stable before the edge; hold time specifies how long it must remain stable afterward, under the characterized conditions. A violation can cause metastability or incorrect capture.

Protocol interfaces show why syntax alone is insufficient at the behavioral level as well, since a model can generate a plausible token sequence that wires the wrong signals, violates an interconnect handshake, drops a reset condition, or references a stale module hierarchy. If a generated Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) Stream bridge must throttle its upstream sender when its first-in, first-out (FIFO) buffer fills but omits the `tready` backpressure path, a lightly loaded simulation without congestion may miss the defect, whereas traffic bursts that exceed the receiver's service and buffering capacity will overflow the buffer and lose data.[^fn-backpressure-c04] Whether omitting `tready` is actually a bug depends on the interface contract, because a receiver guaranteed to accept every transfer need not provide the signal, and training on additional superficially similar text examples does not establish that a generated bridge satisfies its flow-control obligations. Usable representations must therefore preserve both the circuit structure and the contextual contracts that allow verification tools and reviewers to catch such mistakes before silicon fabrication.

[^fn-backpressure-c04]: **Backpressure**: A mechanism, such as AXI Stream's `tready` signal, that lets a receiver pause upstream transfers. A receiver that cannot always accept arriving traffic needs backpressure or another flow-control arrangement. Without sufficient service, buffering, or flow control, sustained excess arrivals can overflow finite buffers and lose data.

Although representation choice and automation scope are distinct engineering decisions, the chosen representation bounds what an automated loop can observe and change. Because flat token streams do not expose concurrency, clock domains, or physical constraints directly, a workflow that sees only text must either recover those relationships or leave them to downstream checks. A search over a fixed parameter schema requires only the tunable parameters and the template around them, whereas a system proposing coordinated edits across software loop nests, memory hierarchies, and hardware netlists needs IRs that link all three levels to physical feedback.

Compiler frameworks supply that multi-level structure by pairing parameter schemas and control-data flow graphs with typed IRs. Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) defines modular dialects across abstraction levels, and Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) applies that infrastructure to hardware design [@CIRCT].[^fn-hardware-ssa-c04] When a flow lowers high-level tensor operations (`linalg`) or affine loop nests (`affine`) into structural hardware dialects (`comb` and `seq`), it must perform explicit high-level synthesis scheduling, resource sharing, and arbitration of memory ports and banks to avoid access conflicts. Static type checks across these dialects can reject malformed transformations and incompatible operands early, while functional correctness and physical realization still require checks that static types cannot express.

[^fn-hardware-ssa-c04]: **Static single assignment (SSA) in hardware IRs**: Software IRs such as LLVM use SSA form, in which each variable is assigned exactly once. In CIRCT's `hw`, `comb`, and `seq` dialects, SSA values represent wires or buses rather than sequential software variables, so single assignment gives every wire one driver. Module bodies are graph regions that do not impose SSA dominance, so cyclic connections can be written; combinational loops are caught by dedicated checking passes rather than by the SSA form itself.

Linear text also separates a signal's declaration from the statements that read or drive it. This is a concrete representation cost: a method trying to modify a handshake must recover the relevant connections even when their source locations are far apart. A parse of public benchmark RTL, hardware libraries, and RISC-V cores compares that separation in token order with the path between the same declaration and use in a syntax tree (@fig-ch04-spatial-semantic-dilation) [@Slang; @VerilogEval; @RTLLM; @Taylor2018BaseJumpSTL; @Kindgren2018SERV; @LowRISCIbex; @Wolf2015PicoRV32].

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Inline values come from the same per-file CSV used by the figure.
# Source: data/studies/09-representation-dilation/measure_representation_dilation.py
import csv as _csv4d
import re as _re4d
from pathlib import Path as _Path4d

import numpy as _np4d
import _python.plots as _ap4d

_root4d = _Path4d(_ap4d.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
_path4d = (
    _root4d / "book" / "contents" / "chapters" / "04-representations"
    / "data" / "fig-hardware-representation-dilation.csv"
)


class _Raw4d:
    """Render inline without quotes, so Quarto emits the text unescaped."""

    def __init__(self, text):
        self.text = text

    def __repr__(self):
        return self.text


with open(_path4d, encoding="utf-8") as _fh:
    _lines4d = _fh.read().splitlines()
_rows4d = list(_csv4d.DictReader(l for l in _lines4d if not l.startswith("#")))
_meas4d = [r for r in _rows4d if r["status"] == "measured"]
_ver4d = _re4d.search(r"pyslang (\S+?)\.\s", "\n".join(_lines4d[:3])).group(1)


def _fit4d(rows, key="mean_token_distance", reps=10_000, seed=20260929):
    """Log-log OLS slope with a percentile bootstrap over files (as the study)."""
    rows = [r for r in rows if r[key] != ""]
    x = _np4d.log10([float(r["tokens"]) for r in rows])
    y = _np4d.log10([float(r[key]) for r in rows])
    slope = _np4d.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0]
    rng = _np4d.random.default_rng(seed)
    boots = [_np4d.polyfit(x[i], y[i], 1)[0] for i in (rng.integers(0, x.size, x.size) for _ in range(reps))]
    lo, hi = _np4d.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
    return slope, lo, hi


dil_measured = len(_meas4d)
dil_tree_files = sum(bool(r["mean_tree_distance"]) for r in _meas4d)
dil_tree_pairs = _Raw4d(f"{sum(int(r['tree_pairs']) for r in _meas4d):,}")
dil_pyslang = _Raw4d(_ver4d)
dil_slope, dil_slope_lo, dil_slope_hi = (
    _Raw4d(f"{v:.2f}") for v in _fit4d(_meas4d)
)
```

The measurement uses pyslang's name lookup to connect in-file signal references to their resolved declarations. Token distance counts the intervening lexical tokens; tree distance counts edges along the syntax-tree path between the same nodes. This convenience corpus covers `{python} dil_measured` measured files at pinned commits. Unresolved names and missing syntax nodes limit the recovered pairs, and the tree measurement covers only the subset for which both endpoints are available.[^fn-dilation-sampling-c04]

[^fn-dilation-sampling-c04]: **Measurement scope**: The original file-selection rule for the BaseJump and Ibex subsets was not recorded. Required BaseJump parameters were set to 4 for elaboration. Bootstrap intervals resample files within this corpus; related files and shared templates limit their interpretation as evidence about hardware beyond it.

![**Token separation grows with file length; syntax-tree paths remain short.** (a) Mean declaration-to-use distance in tokens has a log-log slope of `{python} dil_slope` (95% bootstrap interval `{python} dil_slope_lo` to `{python} dil_slope_hi`). (b) Tree paths cover `{python} dil_tree_pairs` pairs in `{python} dil_tree_files` files; a def-use graph links each pair directly. Parsed with pyslang `{python} dil_pyslang` [@Slang; @VerilogEval; @RTLLM].](images/fig-hardware-representation-dilation){#fig-ch04-spatial-semantic-dilation width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel log-log scatter chart of declaration-to-use distance against file length in tokens for several hundred hardware source files from six corpora, each drawn with its own marker shape, hollow for benchmark files and filled for production files. (a) Mean distance in tokens rises along a fitted line that tracks file length, from the smallest benchmark files to the largest generated library file. (b) Mean path length in syntax-tree edges for the subset with recoverable tree paths stays in a narrow, nearly flat band across the whole range, above a dashed line at one edge marking the def-use graph."}

The difference follows from what each representation connects. A token sequence separates a declaration from its uses by all the intervening source text, so that separation grows as a module grows. A syntax-tree path instead follows the nesting of declarations, statements, and blocks. A definition-use graph connects each declaration directly to its uses, making that dependency explicit regardless of source-file length. CIRCT's SSA operands provide this direct connectivity for transformations that must preserve which values feed which operations.

These measurements illustrate access to a relationship, not a demonstrated advantage for a particular learned model. Context length and training affect whether a sequence model can recover distant dependencies, and a graph's short paths do not establish correct handshakes or physical timing. The useful design choice is which relationships to expose directly and which to recover through additional sources and checks. That choice changes again as the design moves between abstraction levels.

### Abstraction Levels and Tool Inputs

CIRCT and MLIR represent computation across progressive abstraction levels [@CIRCT], and each lowering step makes some properties explicit while discarding others. A loop schedule's array bounds and induction variables are explicit in a structured loop dialect such as `affine`, but disappear once the design is lowered to register-level dialects such as `seq`. A method that modifies the loop schedule after observing a timing violation at the register level therefore needs a link back to the abstraction level where those loop bounds live.

The same trade-off appears across the wider hardware and software stack (@tbl-representation-formats). Source descriptions and compiler dialects (such as SystemVerilog [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog], Flexible Intermediate Representation for RTL (FIRRTL), and typed CIRCT dialects [@CIRCT; @Izraelevitz2017Chisel]) make hierarchy, types, and transformation rules explicit, whereas structural representations such as and-inverter graphs (AIGs) and technology-mapped gate netlists strip away high-level control to expose Boolean logic nodes or cell pins. Neither group carries its full physical or dynamic context on its own. Gate-level timing still depends on cell libraries, interconnect models, and companion Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) and Unified Power Format (UPF) files [@SynopsysSDC; @IEEE2024UPF],[^fn-timing-exceptions-c04] while microarchitectural traces from ChampSim or Ramulator 2 record only the memory events exposed by a particular capture setup.

[^fn-timing-exceptions-c04]: **Timing exceptions**: In static timing analysis, `set_false_path` excludes specified path checks, for example on logically unreachable paths, while `set_multicycle_path` changes the launch/capture edge relationship for paths allowed multiple clock cycles. Improperly constructed timing exceptions in automated flows can cause catastrophic silent failures by declaring failing critical paths as false paths.

| **Artifact or representation** | **What it makes explicit** | **What requires additional information or checks** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Specification, architectural goals, or block diagram | Required behavior, interfaces, system boundaries, and intended organization. | Ambiguous requirements, current applicability, and whether an implementation satisfies the intent. |
| Workload description, design note, or review rationale | Expected use, assumptions, alternatives, and reasons for a decision. | Captured runtime behavior and the evidence supporting each judgment. |
| Software compiler IR | Operations, control/data dependencies, and supported scheduling or mapping choices. | Properties outside that abstraction, including physical timing and workload-dependent stalls. |
| SystemVerilog / VHDL source | Logic, hierarchy, interfaces, types, and parameters interpreted through elaboration. | External contracts, untested behavior, and physical properties supplied by other sources. |
| Typed hardware IR (FIRRTL, CIRCT) | Operations, types, connectivity, and supported transformations. | Whether the desired change is expressible, preserves behavior, and can be implemented. |
| Gate netlist or and-inverter graph (AIG) | Cell connections or Boolean logic structure. | High-level intent, cell-library context, electrical delay, and layout. |
| Parameter schema / generator | Mutable parameters, legal values, and a path to generated artifacts. | Whether dependent files update consistently and the resulting candidate passes its checks. |
| SDC and UPF constraints | Timing and power intent, domains, and implementation assumptions. | Stale hierarchical paths, waived checks, and consistency with the current RTL. |
| Memory or microarchitectural trace | Events observed during a particular execution. | Uncaptured phases, changed software, and timing feedback absent from the trace. |
| Graph, spatial, or cross-layer view | Connectivity, adjacency, location, or links between abstraction levels. | Relationships omitted from nodes and edges, and a path back to tool inputs. |
| Learned embedding | Task-dependent learned features and similarity. | Exact identity, structure, units, legality, and check status unless supplied separately. |
: **Every representation exposes some properties and leaves others to linked sources and checks.** The choice affects both which changes a method can express and which consequences it can inspect. {#tbl-representation-formats tbl-colwidths="[22,34,44]"}

A block diagram and a gate netlist, for example, can describe the same design while supporting different edits. The diagram exposes a shared-memory organization; the netlist exposes cell connections. Neither automatically preserves the relationship between a high-level memory choice and the paths created by its implementation. Links across these views are therefore part of the representation, not optional documentation added after a search. Learned embeddings compress the information further, trading exact structure for task-specific features.

### Code, Graph, and Workload Embeddings

Discrete syntax trees, compiler graphs, and gate-level netlists preserve exact types and wiring, but their variable size and combinatorial structure can make similarity retrieval and prediction expensive. A learned *embedding* maps selected information into a numeric vector whose coordinates capture task-specific relationships. It supplies a compact view rather than an exact replacement for the artifact. Code passages, circuit graphs, and workload behavior can all supply inputs to vector representations, although some vectors are computed features rather than learned embeddings:

1. **Code and document embeddings ($\mathbf{z}_{\text{code}} \in \mathbb{R}^n$):** Learned vectors derived from tokens, syntax trees, or source passages for retrieval and downstream code tasks. ChipNeMo's retrieval component illustrates how project material can support engineering assistance [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo].
2. **Circuit and graph embeddings ($\mathbf{z}_{\text{graph}} \in \mathbb{R}^m$):** Graph neural network representations over AIGs, cell connectivity graphs, MLIR spatial dialects, and physical floorplan adjacency matrices (such as DeepGate2 and learned macro-placement canvas graphs) that encode topology, logic depth, and physical proximity.
3. **Workload and trace vectors ($\mathbf{z}_{\text{trace}} \in \mathbb{R}^k$):** Encodings of runtime behavior from instruction streams, memory access histograms, or DRAM command logs. SimPoint basic block vectors ($w_{\text{BBV}}$) are an example of computed features; a learned encoder can produce a different compact view.

Nearby vectors may retrieve similar schedules or circuits without guaranteeing compatible interfaces or satisfied timing constraints. Retrieval therefore returns the underlying source along with its similarity score. A workflow that proposes changes in the learned space also needs a way to map the proposal back to explicit compiler inputs or hardware artifacts that tools can construct and check.

Graph-based encodings illustrate which structural relationships a learned vector can draw from directly. Graph representations preserve fan-in, fan-out, connectivity, and logic locality at the node level, as demonstrated in DeepGate2's learned representations over AIGs [@ShiEtAl2023DeepGate2]. Similarly, learned macro placement represents chips through connectivity graphs paired with spatial grid canvases [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement], though both graph and canvas structures remain derived views of the native placement state rather than independent sources of truth.

### State for Multi-Step Design

Because embeddings and graph views are derived projections, a sequence of candidate edits needs an explicit state representation to track what changes after each action. A vector used for a one-time similarity query does not, by itself, specify how to construct the next design or update its workload context. Multi-step planning therefore pairs explicit design and environment state with any learned vectors used to predict the consequences of an action, while recording the checks required before a predicted successor becomes a usable candidate.

When multi-step planning is required, predictive methods estimate how an action updates that state (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization). The representation must first distinguish the candidate from the conditions under which it will operate. We express that distinction as:

$$s = \left\langle s_{\text{design}}, s_{\text{env}} \right\rangle$$

- **Design and software state ($s_{\text{design}}$):** The candidate hardware organization and software choices, including compiler schedules. A parameter search can use a vector $\theta \in \Theta$ within a fixed template; a structural change needs the relevant compiler IRs or hardware graphs and links to the interfaces it affects.
- **Environment and operating-condition state ($s_{\text{env}}$):** The workload, operating conditions, and constraints against which the candidate is evaluated.
